brief: The pin's 100 MHz is the AXI clock's rounding of 50 MHz (mainline gcc-msm8998 has no 50 MHz entry), reported while clock scaling is idle-suspended; the pin is the low state, not a refusal
question: Why does 'userspace + set_freq 50000000' read back cur_freq 100000000 on our v7.3 kernel (runs 6 and 7), what does that mean for the link, and what must step 16 assert?
found:
Read only, from our tree topic/ufs-match-android 0f3429f65ce4 (v7.3, the matched image's) and the local tag reference/android-walleye/4.4.302-g113bd1cfa6f5; runs 6 and 7 (lab-material ufs-20261124-000728, -001519) both read 'simple_ondemand, clock 50000000' before and 'userspace, clock 100000000' after, gear HS_GEAR1 before. No phone.
(1) The path. set_freq_store sets user_frequency=50000000 and calls update_devfreq -> devfreq_update_target, which only clamps to the node's min/max (50 MHz..200 MHz, the two OPPs ufshcd_devfreq_init adds from core_clk's freq-table-hz, since msm8998 has no operating-points-v2 so use_pm_opp=false): 50 MHz passes. devfreq_set_target calls ufshcd_devfreq_target, which FIRST overrides *freq = clk_round_rate(core_clk, 50 MHz) (ufshcd.c 1609-1612). core_clk is GCC_UFS_AXI_CLK, CLK_SET_RATE_PARENT on ufs_axi_clk_src, whose mainline table is 100/200/240 MHz - no 50 MHz - and rcg2 rounds up: *freq = 100 MHz. Then, if hba->clk_scaling.is_suspended (it is at idle: ufshcd_clk_scaling_suspend_work suspends scaling when a window ends with no requests), it warns 'clock scaling is suspended, skip' and returns 0 with *freq still 100 MHz (1620-1624). devfreq_set_target stores previous_freq = 100 MHz, and cur_freq_show prints previous_freq (ufs-qcom's profile has no get_cur_freq). Nothing in the hardware changed. Had scaling been active, scale_up = (100 MHz == max 200 MHz) is false, *freq = clki->min_freq = 50 MHz, scaling-not-required (already down): previous_freq 50 MHz. So 100 MHz is bookkeeping of the skipped request, not a clock change and not a refusal.
(2) The 50 MHz one check earlier is the same bookkeeping: the last real scale-down (simple_ondemand, scaling active) handed back min_freq. clki->curr_freq is also the requested min_freq, never clk_get_rate. The real core clock at the 'low' OPP on our kernel is 100 MHz always: clk_set_rate(core_clk, 50 MHz) sets the RCG's ceiling entry, 100 MHz. Android's clock-gcc-8998.c table has 50 MHz, so Android's low state runs core_clk at 50 MHz; ours at 100 MHz. A difference from Android, NOT KNOWN YET whether it matters to the silent load (not shown to).
(3) Android 4.4.302, the same two writes: its ufshcd_devfreq_target accepts only 0 (down) or UINT_MAX (up) and returns -EINVAL 'invalid freq' for 50000000; it registers no OPPs. So 'set_freq 50000000' FAILS on Android; the way there is set_freq 0. This corrects research walleye-ufs-hold-the-clock-read §4 ('on both trees'): the 50 MHz write is mainline's way only.
(4) Gear: on the legacy path the gear follows the scale-up/down state, not the number: scale-down sets clk_scaling.min_gear = HS_G1. The read 100 MHz is the low state, HS-G1 on this card (gear-before HS_GEAR1 in runs 6 and 7); it is not G3. Under userspace the governor keeps requesting 50 MHz, so when load resumes scaling (resume_work -> update_devfreq) the target is scale-down again: no scale-up while userspace holds 50 MHz.
What step 16 must assert: NOT cur_freq == 50000000 (it reads 100 MHz at idle by the rounding above, 50 MHz once scaling is active), NOT min_freq (the QoS floor, untouched by the write, proves nothing). Assert the setting that holds and the state it gives: governor reads 'userspace', userspace/set_freq reads 50000000, and power_info gear reads HS_GEAR1; cur_freq is printed and accepted as either the lowest OPP (50000000) or that OPP's rounding by core_clk (100000000), never 200000000. On a node without userspace (max_freq path), max_freq reads back 50000000 and the same gear.
The next run must capture, before the governor write, after it and after set_freq: governor, available_governors, available_frequencies, min_freq, max_freq, cur_freq, userspace/set_freq, trans_stat, power_info gear/mode/lane; dmesg AFTER the write (the 'clock scaling is suspended, skip' line proves this read directly - runs 6 and 7's dmesg.txt was taken at boot, before the write); and /sys/kernel/debug/clk/gcc_ufs_axi_clk/clk_rate where debugfs is mounted (NOT KNOWN YET whether it is in the run's ramdisk), which should read 100000000 at the low state.
NOT KNOWN YET: the warning line itself (not captured); the hardware clk_rate; whether the 100 MHz vs Android's 50 MHz core clock bears on the silence under load.

brief: rw run 1 had no gadget because the init refused its own command line: walleye.booted-slot with root system_a while booted from memory on slot b; nothing was mounted
question: Why did the rw-write image, booted from memory in run 1, bring up no USB gadget (check 14), and what tells the causes apart before run 2?
found:
Cause, from the code and a count (not from a hardware capture): the rw-write image cb79c975 was made from the STAGE 2 production image, whose command line carries walleye.booted-slot (read 2026-11-24 from the image's own header: "clk_ignore_unused ignore_loglevel panic=5 androidboot.hardware=walleye androidboot.dtbo_idx=3 walleye.root=system_a walleye.booted-slot walleye.rw"). The rw write boots it the STAGE 1 way: fastboot boot from memory while Android's slot b stays current, root the other slot's system_a, and the run adds androidboot.slot_suffix=_b (rootfs_boot::run_cmdline). The init (build/initramfs-root-rw-write/init lines 131-134) then requires ROOT = system$SLOT under walleye.booted-slot: system_a is not system_b, so it refuses "walleye.booted-slot: system_a is not the system of the booted slot" BEFORE any mount, pauses 30 s petting the watchdog, and does reboot -f. That fits every measure of run 1: no gadget for 145 s, the phone back on Android slot b by itself, the card and boot chain equal. Counted: tests/host/ufs-root-rw-init.sh passes 2026-11-24 (30 s, QEMU); its case R3 "booted-slot with a root that is not the booted slot's" boots exactly run 1's line (walleye.root=system_a androidboot.slot_suffix=_b walleye.rw walleye.booted-slot) and sees that refusal. Its R1 (the rw success case) has no walleye.booted-slot, which is why the QEMU proof passed while the image could not work; the rehearsal never boots, so nothing caught it. The item's candidates (a) rw mount refused, (b) OpenRC or the gadget unit on a rw root, (c) the self-reboot racing a slow boot are not reached: the init stops before the mount. They stay not known until a boot gets past the guard.
NOT captured on hardware: the refusal line was in ramoops after run 1, but Android rebooted since (uptime 664 s at 14:10, read by adb as shell; no root, so pstore was not read). Instrument for run 2: the refusal path is a warm reboot -f, which keeps console-ramoops (research walleye-stop-pstore-reads-runs-4-and-7-three-answers: only a PMIC bite empties it), so a no-gadget stop reads /sys/fs/pstore from Android AT ONCE, before any reboot, and tells apart: a "walleye-ufs-root: refused ..." line (a guard, which one), "handing over to the root's /sbin/init" with no gadget (cause b or c), "mounts-rw" without hand-over (cause a), nothing (no start or a bite).
Failing test: tools/walleye-tries/src/rw_write.rs the_rw_image_command_line_passes_the_inits_slot_guard_when_booted_from_memory (ignored so main stays green; cargo test --lib -- --ignored shows it failing on cb79c975).

brief: The image's shutdown level has killprocs and savecache but NO mount-ro; remount over a live ssh/syslog session is busy by design; a QEMU test reproduces run 3 and passes with killprocs then mount-ro
question: What holds the rw Alpine root open so mount -o remount,ro / says busy, and how does Alpine itself end a rw root?
found: (1) rootfs/runlevels: 'shutdown killprocs' and 'shutdown savecache' only; Alpine's own shutdown level also has mount-ro (after killprocs), which is what ends a rw root. (2) The run's end does not use it: settle_rw (tools/walleye-tries/src/rootfs_boot.rs, SETTLE_COMMAND) runs sync and mount -o remount,ro / inside a live ssh session, then walleye-reboot --command bootloader (a reboot syscall, no init shutdown). A remount ro is refused EBUSY while any process has a file of the root open for writing, so the live syslog (/var/log/messages, wtmp from utmps, seedrng, the ssh session) is enough; settled.txt of run 3 shows /var/log/messages and wtmp written. Not captured on the phone: which exact process held it (nothing was changed on the phone). (3) tests/host/rw-root-clean-end.sh (QEMU, rw-write init, writer holding /var/log/messages open, busybox init, the image's own inittab shutdown line, a stub openrc reading the shutdown level of rootfs/runlevels): today it FAILS with e2fsck -fn 'Free blocks count wrong (11490, counted=11488)' and 'skipping journal recovery' - run 3's own signature; with a level of mount-ro alone the remount says 'Device or resource busy'; with killprocs then mount-ro it remounts ro and e2fsck -fn is clean (passes). (4) Hazards seen: killprocs also kills the hold script and the petters (busybox watchdog's SIGTERM writes the magic close, disarming the watchdog), so the end must finish by itself in a reboot; and busybox init's own final reboot is a plain restart, not to the bootloader, so the bootloader step has to be a shutdown service after mount-ro. A stub's own file open on the root (a redirect to /tmp) also made the remount busy: the end's own tools write to /run only.

brief: WDT0-read image built: the production init plus a walleye.wdt0 first act that reads EN, STS, BARK_TIME, BITE_TIME with devmem, read only; image 17a9c21d rebuilt equal by image ensure; never booted
question: Can the production UFS-root image read WDT0 at its first instant, read only, and keep the four values where the lab reads them over ssh, behind one word, with the ro image untouched?
found: build/initramfs-root-wdt0/init is build/initramfs-root-production/init with WDT0 blocks (cut them and the file is the production init, line for line). With walleye.wdt0 the init's FIRST act after /proc, /sys, /dev (before the petters, the command line's other words, the slot and the card) reads 0x17817008 EN, 0x1781700c STS, 0x17817010 BARK_TIME, 0x17817014 BITE_TIME with 'devmem ADDR 32' (two arguments: no value is ever given, no write to any watchdog register); offsets are WDT0_EN 0x08, WDT0_STS 0x0C, WDT0_BARK_TIME 0x10, WDT0_BITE_TIME 0x14 of android:drivers/soc/qcom/watchdog_v2.c@113bd1cfa6f5 lines 39-42 on base 0x17817000. Each value goes to the kernel log as 'walleye-wdt0: NAME ADDR VALUE' (or FAILED and devmem's words, the next register still read) and to /tmp/wdt0.log, which the hand-over copies to /.walleye/wdt0 and /run/walleye/wdt0 of the root (the ro overlay in memory: nothing written to the card). tests/host/wdt0-init.sh (W0-W5) passes on the init, fails on the production init; the root init's whole QEMU proof (ufs-root-init.sh) passes with this init in its place. Image: control production b74af863, ramdisk 17d4286b872e3bbc2c7a5631a09f262eec636a864e085e626988767ba97439d7, cmdline = production's without walleye.booted-slot, plus walleye.wdt0 (the try boots from memory on the other slot): sha256 17a9c21d75ebb046e90abafac322e865d3bcbb7f90a262543e5c6b72a061f642, built twice equal by build/build-ufs-root-wdt0.sh (21 checks) and rebuilt equal from its recipe by lpoco-bringup image ensure (store path deleted between); the header equals the recipe. Never booted. Not known yet: whether our kernel's /dev/mem allows the read at 0x17817000 (a refusal is said as FAILED with devmem's words, not hidden), what the bootloader armed.

brief: WDT0 at our kernel's first instant (kernel log of run 1): EN 0, STS 0, BARK 0x7FFFF, BITE 0xFFFFF - bootloader leaves it disarmed

brief: Suspected: the adb stream's rate varies (8.8 MB/s, a stall on 16 MiB, 120 KB/s) on one card; the digest is now made on the phone
question: Why did the adb read of system_a take 760 s+ on 2026-11-25 when rootfs-boots run 7 read it in 306 s?
found: Run 7 (research/walleye-display-s6e3fa5/2026-11-23/rootfs-boots-run-7.log): check 7 306 s for 2684354560 bytes = 8.8 MB/s. Stage 2 run 6 (stage2-run6-stall.txt): a read of boot_a (16 MiB) stalled, dd in wait_woken (blocked writing the adb pipe). Keeper 2026-11-25-0830: 120 KB/s, usb 480 Mb/s. Three rates and a stall on one card point at the exec-out stream, but it is a HYPOTHESIS: a phone-side dd to /dev/null and sha256sum timing would split card from stream. Built: dd | sha256sum on the phone, with dd's own status echoed (dd=0 required; exec-out carries no exit status), time-only bound. To confirm on the phone by the keeper: that adb kill after a stall leaves no dd running (ps), and that sha256sum exists on this Android (the GPT read already uses it). The rehearsal's check 7 finishing fast = the stream was slow.

brief: nxp-nci-i2c takes no clock in mainline, and its -121 before nfc0 is opened is the driver's own cold-mode message, not an I2C fault; the OnePlus 5 node (same SoC) is the form to copy
question: How do mainline Qualcomm boards give an NXP NCI chip its clock, and what does nxp-nci's -121 at 1.19 s mean on walleye?
found: The binding nxp,nci.yaml has no clocks property (additionalProperties false). drivers/nfc/nxp-nci/i2c.c gets only the enable gpio (GPIOD_OUT_LOW, l.299) and an optional firmware gpio (l.305). In COLD mode, before nfc0 is opened, the IRQ thread sets -EREMOTEIO itself and prints Read failed (l.224-226), and set_mode clears hard_fault (l.56). So the -121 says only that gpio92 was high while the chip was off. No mainline qcom board models the NFC clock (msm8998-oneplus-common.dtsi:207-218, sdm845-oneplus-common.dtsi:493, sdm845-google-common.dtsi:398, sm8150-sony-xperia-kumano.dtsi:496, sdm632-fairphone-fp3.dts:146); the clock runs on PMIC hardware clkreq. sm7325-nothing-spacewar holds a TLMM clkreq pin by pinctrl. RPM_SMD_LN_BB_CLK3_PIN exists for msm8998 (clk-smd-rpm.c:1015) and is used by no NFC node. The OnePlus 5 (msm8998, the same Android layout: irq 92, pinctrl 12 and 116 pulled up) reads tags with enable-gpios = tlmm 116, no firmware gpio, and pinctrl pull-ups on 12, 116 and 92 (Kettunen 2022, https://lkml.iu.edu/2202.3/02782.html). Tell the causes apart with nfc0 opened (nfctool -d nfc0 -1): no ACK at 0x28 means VEN; an ACK and no NCI reply means the clock; firmware framing means gpio93 polarity. Researcher subagent of the walleye coordinator, 2026-11-26, read against the local 7.3 source.

brief: DEV_UP rc=0 is the PN553's own reply: nci_open_device returns 0 only after CORE_RESET, CORE_INIT and init-complete responses came back over i2c
question: Run 2 acked NFC_CMD_DEV_UP (rc=0) but 0x28 was not probed: did the chip answer?
found: net/nfc/nci/core.c nci_open_device (linux-phone-oco/linux HEAD): after ops->open (nxp-nci: VEN up) it runs __nci_request(nci_reset_req), ops->setup, __nci_request(nci_init_req), post_setup, __nci_request(nci_init_complete_req); each waits on req_completion, which only a response packet from the chip completes (nci_rsp_packet), else -ETIMEDOUT and cleanup. NCI_UP is set and 0 returned only if all three answered. So run 2's ack (research walleye-nfc-boot-run-2) measures that the PN553 answered NCI over i2c at 0x28 with VEN high, gpio93 low, BBCLK3 unused: VEN, the bus and firmware mode are not the fault, and the chip runs without that clock at least to init. A plain i2c read of 0x28 would add nothing and races the bound driver (it needs -f). Not known yet: RF - whether a poll finds a tag. brief: walleye-nfc-up --poll SECONDS: START_POLL after DEV_UP on one held socket; static aarch64 ab2cf4c1, NFC ramdisk f4b6c1d7 and image 019b0dce rebuild equal, UFS-off passes
question: Can walleye-nfc-up poll for a target after DEV_UP and say 'target found' or 'no target', and does the NFC image still rebuild equal?
found: tools/walleye-nfc-up --poll SECONDS (argenv, env WALLEYE_NFC_UP_POLL, default 0 = no poll): after DEV_UP acks, it asks the controller for family nfc and its multicast group "events" (CTRL_ATTR_MCAST_GROUPS), opens ONE socket that joins the group before anything is sent (the kernel stops a poll when the socket that started it closes, and events go to the group), sends NFC_CMD_START_POLL (DEVICE_INDEX, IM_PROTOCOLS 0xfe = every initiator protocol), waits up to SECONDS for NFC_EVENT_TARGETS_FOUND of that device, then NFC_CMD_STOP_POLL when none came (a found target ends the poll in the kernel). Prints 'nfc0: poll N s: target found (NFC_EVENT_TARGETS_FOUND)' or 'nfc0: poll N s: no target'; an errno to START_POLL is an error, exit 1. Numbers are the v7.3 uapi nfc.h and genetlink.h, pinned by a test (libc for the genetlink ones). Tests: 15 unit tests (stand-in kernel: join the group the controller named events not other, target ends it, no target is stopped and waited its time, an event of another device or kind is no target, START_POLL errno stops before the wait, request layout) and one against this host's real kernel (its nfc family lists group events, a socket joins it and reads nothing in 20 ms); 7 binary tests (dry run adds the poll step, poll not a number refused). The procedure nfc-boot-on-the-pixel-2 runs walleye-nfc-up --index 0 --poll 10 under timeout 30; open_judge reads the tool's two poll words into OpenAnswer.poll (target, no target, or not run when the open stopped first, never 'no target') and the verdict for rc=0 says the chip answered NCI init (DEV_UP is acked only after CORE_RESET and CORE_INIT, research walleye-nfc-dev-up-ack-is-the-chips-reply); a test with the tool's own words; 492 tests of the steps crate pass. Build: build-nfc-up-bin.sh twice = ab2cf4c1 (was 04edd61f); build-initramfs.sh phone with it twice = ramdisk f4b6c1d7; control: the same script with the old binary reproduces 973bcb87 and without EXTRA_BIN b094adc1, so the instrument is on its known case; lpoco-bringup image ensure nfc --rebuild twice: image 019b0dce (was 65cef2f5), declared in device.toml with the recipe's ramdisk; tests/host/ufs-off-image.sh passes on it. NOT RUN ON THE PHONE: the aarch64 file has not executed anywhere; no tag was held to a reader here, so 'target found' has never been seen on real input (the first run is walleye-nfc-poll-run-no-tag, the known case 'no target'). Not read: the target's own data (GET_TARGET: protocols, NFCID1), left out on purpose. Review by the programmer subagent fixed before landing: a START_POLL errno after a good DEV_UP is a failed poll with cause 'answered' (not the clock); events that come between a request and its answer are kept for the wait; a refused STOP_POLL is said; --poll above 3600 s is refused; the host kernel test returns when the host has no nfc family. The seq pick in the socket's exchange has no test of its own (needs a real socket pair).

brief: C1 settles it: slot a's bootloader path cuts the tail for any image; C2 and C3 are void by their own rule; the cut is harmless while root=PARTUUID, no check left
question: What is left to check after C1's cut on slot a (RAM boot, 1141 chars, ends at androidboot.pk, no slot_suffix)?
found: The plan in cmdline-cut-checks.md (research walleye-cmdline-tail-cut-candidates) reads C1 as: cut at pk means the slot-a path cuts whatever the image. C1 ran exactly that: a RAM-booted debug image (149-char header, not flashed) was cut on slot a (run 20261125-085235). So the cause is on the bootloader side with slot a current, not our header, kernel, ramdisk, DTB or footer; C2 (stock image flashed to boot_a) was only for a whole tail and is void; C3 (our image with stock header fields flashed to boot_a) could only separate header fields from sizes, which a RAM boot with a different header already did not change, and it needs a boot_a flash for no gain. Nothing the cmdline's slot words carry is needed: step 21 takes the slot from root=PARTUUID (run 12 passed that way). Cause stays not proven (the bootloader is closed and not read); it is recorded as known-unexplained, not broken. Reopen only if something needs androidboot.slot_suffix or words after pk (then read it from slot b, where the line is whole, or flip the question to why slot b is whole). No phone work queued.

brief: PON reasons after a bite: read raw 0xC0..0xCB in our image via fastboot after one vol-down+power hold; Android getprop second; a no-bite control read first settles what a key press leaves
question: How are PON_REASON1, PON_ON_REASON, POFF_REASON1 and WARM_RESET_REASON1 read after a watchdog bite on walleye, given the charger screen has no adb and Android's dmesg is already a second boot?
found: READ this session in the vendor msm driver (qpnp-power-on.c, whole file fetched): PM8998 is PON gen2; offsets PON_REASON1 0xC0, WARM_RESET_REASON1 0xC2, POFF_REASON1 0xC5, PON_OFF_REASON 0xC7, FAULT_REASON1 0xC8, S3_RESET_REASON 0xCA (gen1: 0x08, 0x0A, 0x0C). This settles the offsets the earlier row left open: the driver has no separate PON_ON_REASON register - warm vs cold is WARM_RESET_REASON1 non-zero (qpnp_pon_is_warm_reset). On gen2 the driver reads 0xC7 first and only then POFF_REASON1 (0xC5, bit 2 = PMIC_WD per mainline), FAULT_REASON1 (0xC8/0xC9) or S3_RESET_REASON (0xCA), by which of the POFF_SEQ/FAULT_SEQ/S3_RESET_SEQ bits is set; a procedure reading only 0xC5 can miss a bite recorded elsewhere, so read 0xC0..0xCB raw. At probe the vendor driver stores WARM_RESET_REASON then clears it: the first Linux that probes the PON eats it, so Android's kernel after the press shows the warm bit once and a later reader sees zero; reading in our image before Android boots keeps it. It logs 'Power-on reason: X and cold/warm boot' and 'Power-off reason: Y' at probe (Android's own reading; needs dmesg access, which a user build may refuse). WAYS: (a) phone returns by itself (warm bite): adb getprop ro.boot.bootreason / sys.boot.reason, no hand; (b) charger screen or off, nothing answers, so ONE physical act: power+volume-down hold to the bootloader (fastboot lists the phone), then fastboot boot of our reader image (a jump, not a PMIC reset - recalled, to confirm) reads 0xC0..0xCB raw through regmap debugfs; (c) a plain power press boots Android: only getprop and, if allowed, dmesg lines, and Android's kernel eats the registers first. NOT MEASURED: whether POFF_REASON1/0xC7/WARM_RESET_REASON1 survive the bootloader and a key press on this phone, and whether the bootloader clears them. A CONTROL with no bite settles it: power the phone off by a known cause (adb reboot -p, or a hold-down hard reset), then path (b), read the same registers - it counts what a key press and the bootloader leave, at no risk to the phone, the author's hands only for the hold. Not read: mainline qcom-pon.c for a PON reason print, and the bootloader's own boot-reason rule (closed).

brief: The PON peripheral's subtype register is 0x805 and reads 04 (gen2 primary) or 05 (gen2 secondary): the proof pon-block checks; no source names a value for 0x804
question: What does a PM8998-class PON regmap read at its TYPE (0x804) and SUBTYPE (0x805) registers, from driver source, so a reading proves it came from the PON?
found: Mainline drivers/input/misc/pm8941-pwrkey.c (linux-phone-oco/linux HEAD): PON_SUBTYPE 0x05, PON_SUBTYPE_PRIMARY 01, SECONDARY 02, 1REG 03, GEN2_PRIMARY 04, GEN2_SECONDARY 05, GEN3_PBS 08, GEN3_HLOS 09; the driver reads base+0x05 (PON_SUBTYPE) and base+0x01 (PON_REV2) and never base+0x04. The Android msm kernel's drivers/platform/msm/qpnp-power-on.c (android.googlesource.com/kernel/msm, android-7.1.0_r0.2): QPNP_PON_PERPH_SUBTYPE = base+0x05, PON_GEN2_PRIMARY 0x04, PON_GEN2_SECONDARY 0x05, reasons at 0xC0/0xC2/0xC5 only for the gen2 subtypes (is_pon_gen2). So on PM8998 (PON gen2: reasons at 0xC0..) the subtype at 0x805 reads 04 (primary) or 05 (secondary PMIC), and a regmap that reads anything else there is not the PON. The item's TYPE register 0x804: neither driver reads or names a value for it, so pon-block prints it raw (type=VV) and judges nothing by it. NOT KNOWN YET: what 0x804 reads on the phone, and that regmap debugfs shows the PON there at all (the control run).

brief: An OPP table with the msm8998's own clocks cannot hold HS-G3: ufs_qcom_freq_to_gear_speed maps only a 201.5 MHz unipro clock to G3, and the msm8998's top is 150 MHz (G2)
question: Does an operating-points-v2 table on the msm8998 ufshc node, with the freq-table-hz the vendor lists, keep the link at HS-G3 under load (item walleye-ufs-opp-table-image)?
found: Read in the kernel tree wt-k-ufsm (topic/ufs-match-android on v7.3), drivers/ufs/host/ufs-qcom.c ufs_qcom_freq_to_gear_speed (about line 2545): with use_pm_opp true the gear is taken from the OPP's core_clk_unipro entry: 403 MHz G5, 300 MHz G4, 201.5 MHz G3, 150 or 100 MHz G2, 75 or 37.5 MHz G1, any other value logs 'Unsupported clock freq' and returns DONT_CHANGE; the result is capped by the card's max gear. msm8998.dtsi freq-table-hz (line 1040) and the vendor's (research walleye-ufs-hold-the-clock-read: 50/200 MHz core, 37.5/150 MHz unipro) have no 201.5 MHz. So an OPP table of the msm8998's real clocks gives G1 at the low point and G2 at the high point: with it the link would run UNDER load at G2, below the G3 it has now (the legacy path idles at G1 and trains up to the card's gear). The item's proof 'keeps G3' cannot be met by a dts table alone; it needs either a ufs-qcom change that maps 150 MHz to G3 for this SoC (a driver patch with its own review, and whether the PHY and 150 MHz unipro really carry G3 is not known yet: the vendor kernel's gear-with-clock rule was not read, the Android source is not in the commons) or the table as a G1/G2 ladder measured against the legacy path. Not built: no image was made. Source: mainline code only.

brief: Calls need three layers after remoteproc_mss: QMI signalling (ModemManager over qrtr, mainline, now), a SIM, and in-call audio (q6voice, NOT mainline)
question: What does walleye need after remoteproc_mss for calls, in order, and which steps need the author?
found: Layers. (1) Signalling and registration: userspace only. The modem is up (research walleye-modem-mss-first-boot) with qrtr services listed incl. DMS/NAS/WDS/voice ids; libqmi speaks QMI over qrtr and ModemManager (qrtr support, QMI plugin) exposes IMEI, SIM, registration, SMS and the Voice interface (mmcli --voice-create-call). pmOS lists MSM8998 modem Partial, GPS from the modem's PDS works with qrtr alone. rmtfs already served the modem's opens; pd-mapper is in-kernel on new kernels (as on the Mi 9 case); tqftpserv is needed for wlanmdsp.mbn (Wi-Fi), not shown needed for calls; diag-router only if MSS crashes. (2) SIM: nothing registers without one; reading IMEI (DMS get-ids) and the qrtr service set need none. (3) Audio: mainline qdsp6 has the data path only (ASM/AFE/ADM); voice sessions (MVM 0x09, CVS 0x0A, CVP 0x0B) are not upstream. A q6voice series from msm8916-mainline is carried in sdm845-mainline wip/q6voice and sc7280-mainline PR 27; on hardware the call audio is routed modem to codec by the ADSP, a passive control session plus real AFE ports, with q6voiced or a mixer opening the stream. It rests on the ADSP audio path working at all: walleye's tone path (walleye-adsp-q6-mi2s, tas2557) is not proven, so in-call audio comes last. Nobody shows a Pixel 2 doing calls; OnePlus 5 has calls broken. Not known yet: whether the voice QMI service is listed with no SIM, the Pixel 2 earpiece/mic codec route, whether MM crashes the MSS as on OnePlus 5 with the ipa module. Vectors: A QMI/ModemManager first, signalling then audio (chosen); B port q6voice first; C oFono plus q6voiced as on msm8916; D Android RIL via libhybris; E wait for OnePlus 5.

brief: ModemManager runs on walleye from an Alpine aarch64 rootfs pushed into RAM over USB and chrooted; static-in-ramdisk is the fallback
question: Where does ModemManager run on walleye with nothing flashed?
found:
Today's modem image: kernel 15.2 MB + xz ramdisk 8.2 MB in a 32 MiB boot partition, so about 10 MB is free (read from the image header). The firmware (61 MB) is already pushed over the USB network (firmware-recv port 9000) and that works, so a push of more is a proven mechanism. ModemManager (qrtr on by default) finds a qrtr modem through its QrtrBusWatcher, not through udev events, but the daemon still links udev (gudev), dbus and polkit (permissive in Alpine). Alpine edge aarch64 (musl) ships exactly the set pmOS runs: modemmanager 6.7 MB + libmm-glib 1.5 + libqmi 5.5 + glib 5.9 + dbus 0.7 + eudev 1.1 installed, about 25 MB with musl and busybox, roughly 8-10 MB xz. Host has nix, docker and no apk or qemu-user; apk-tools-static x86_64 is on dl-cdn and installs an aarch64 root with --root --arch --no-scripts without running anything of the target.
Ways: (A) static ModemManager built by nix (pkgsStatic musl) into the ramdisk: nothing to push, but static glib/gio/gudev/dbus is unproven, MM must still find dbus-daemon, and the ~10 MB headroom is also needed by later tools; risk high, hours unknown. (B) Alpine aarch64 rootfs tarball built on the host, pushed over USB into RAM (tmpfs), chroot with /proc /sys /dev, /lib/firmware and /rmtfs bind-mounted from the ramdisk; no flash, boot image unchanged except a small push-and-chroot step in modem-up; the packages are pmOS's own. (C) rootfs on the card/UFS: refused by the UFS-off gate. (D) ModemManager on the host over a qrtr tunnel: no mainline qrtr-over-IP in the image, and the product needs it on the phone. (E) skip ModemManager, drive voice with qmicli: qmicli has no voice-call state machine; the item after this needs mmcli.
Chosen: B. Unknown and how each is settled: (1) does musl-Alpine MM start with no udevd and no polkitd - run it in a qemu-free way is impossible on the host, so the first phone try (attended by the keeper, RAM only) reads the log; if polkit is a hard stop, rebuild MM with -Dpolkit=no in nix; (2) dbus system bus in a bare chroot needs /run/dbus, a messagebus user and the MM policy file - all in the tar; (3) RAM headroom: the tar unpacked ~30-40 MB of 4 GB, not a risk; (4) the MM qrtr plugin matching walleye's QMI node - settled by mmcli -L in walleye-modem-mm-sees-modem.

brief: MM 1.24.2 cannot list a QMI modem without a net port; mainline ipa has msm8998 data, no DT node; OnePlus 5 gets the port from 'modprobe ipa'
question: What gives the Pixel 2 modem a net port so ModemManager's qcom-soc plugin lists it?
found: 1) The check is hard in ModemManager 1.24.2 (mm-base-modem.c: qmi && !data_net -> fail); no option, no plugin-side bypass; qcom-soc only accepts the wwan/rpmsg/net/qrtr subsystems and handles bam-dmux net ports. 2) Linux v7.3 has driver and binding for qcom,msm8998-ipa (ipa_data_v3_1), but no msm8998 DT ipa node (msm8998.dtsi has only the ipa_fw_mem/ipa_gsi_mem reserves, which the walleye DT deletes for the phone's own layout). 3) postmarketOS pmaports MR 3531: on the OnePlus 5 the ipa driver is blocked from autoload because of modem stability; 'modprobe ipa' lets ModemManager detect the modem over QRTR (the ipa net device is its net port) and gives working SMS. So the data interface is IPA (v3.1), not BAM-DMUX. Not yet read: the ipa node values (registers, interrupts, iommu, gsi-loader) - they come from the wahoo GPL dtsi and the OnePlus postmarketOS patch; not guessed here. Vectors: A ipa node + CONFIG_QCOM_IPA in the modem test kernel (OnePlus 5 way, mainline driver, upstreamable); B patch ModemManager to allow a QMI modem without a net port (voice/SMS need none; small, upstreamable, but a fork of MM until merged); C a dummy netdev tagged for the plugin (hack, no real data, grouping by physdev unlikely to work over qrtr).

brief: The msm8998 ipa node's values come from wahoo's dtsi and the msm8998-mainline fork; v7.3 has no msm8998 interconnect provider, so dtbs_check says 'interconnects' is required
question: What are the values of the msm8998 ipa node for the modem test kernel, and does it pass the binding?
found: Values and sources are in tests/fixtures/kernel-text/msm8998-ipa-sources.txt. Wahoo (Google, android11 branch): ipa irq SPI 333, gsi irq SPI 432, gsi range 0x1e04000/0x2c000, SMMU stream ids 0x18e0 (ap) and 0x18e2 (uc) on anoc2_smmu, firmware loaded through Trust Zone (pas-id 0xF). The fork (OnePlus 5): ipa-reg 0x1e40000/0x7000, ipa-shared 0x1e47000/0x2000, clock RPM_SMD_IPA_CLK, the smp2p ipa entries, AP loads the firmware (memory-region + firmware-name). The phone's own vendor firmware has ipa_fws.mdt (lab-material vendor-firmware-2026-11-24), so gsi-loader is self. Two findings from dtbs_check in the alpine:edge container: anoc2_smmu has one iommu cell (the fork's two-cell form fails 'too long'); and v7.3 has no msm8998 interconnect provider (no driver, no binding header), so the binding's required 'interconnects' cannot be written: the node has none and the driver gets NULL paths (of_icc_get_by_index returns NULL without the property), running unvoted. The fork carries an interconnect driver (qcom,msm8998.h: bimc, cnoc, snoc, a1noc, a2noc, mnoc) that is not in mainline.

brief: v7.3's ipa driver probes without an interconnects property: of_icc_get gives NULL paths and every bulk call returns 0 on them
question: Does drivers/net/ipa (v7.3) fail probe on an ipa node with no interconnects, as the modem test dts has?
found: No. ipa_interconnect_init (ipa_power.c) calls of_icc_bulk_get, icc_bulk_disable and icc_bulk_set_bw. of_icc_get (drivers/interconnect/core.c) returns NULL when the node has no interconnects property; of_icc_bulk_get (bulk.c) fails only on an ERR_PTR; icc_set_bw and __icc_enable return 0 on a NULL path. So the node probes unvoted. The lines are captured in tests/fixtures/kernel-text/ipa-interconnect-optional-v7.3.txt (git show v7.3:PATH in the kernel clone). dtbs_check's missing-interconnects error stays accepted for this test dtb only; upstream waits on walleye-msm8998-interconnect-provider. NOT KNOWN YET: that the unvoted bus clocks are enough on the phone: the try shows it.
